title: Noun clauses
intro: This unit turns whole sentences into nouns, so that they can be known, said, asked about or judged. `-DIğI` and `-(y)AcAğI` report facts: *Geleceğini biliyorum* (I know you'll come). `-mA` names an action that someone wants or asks for: *Gelmeni istiyorum* (I want you to come). Questions fit inside a sentence the same way: *Nerede oturduğunu bilmiyorum* (I don't know where she lives). And a clause can be the subject: *Gelmen önemli* (It's important that you come).

blocks.text: English says **I know that you came**. Turkish has no word for **that** here: it turns *you came* into a noun with the object participle `-DIk` of [B1 unit 6](gp-participle-dik), adds a possessive for the doer, and gives the whole thing the case the main verb needs: *Geldiğini biliyorum*, literally **I know your having come**.

blocks.title: *gelmek* + *biliyor*: she knows that I came, that you came…

rows.en: she knows that you come (came) (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **Tense.** `-DIk` covers the present and the past: *Ankara'da oturduğunu biliyorum* (I know you live in Ankara), *Dün geldiğini biliyorum* (I know you came yesterday). For the future, use `-(y)AcAk`: *Geleceğini biliyorum* (I know you will come). The main verb keeps its own tense, so *Geleceğini söyledi* is **he said he would come**.

**Negatives, nouns and var.** The negative is `-mAdIk` or `-mAyAcAk`: *gelmediğini*, *gelmeyeceğini*. Nouns and adjectives go through *olmak*, and *değil* becomes *olmadığı*: *Hasta olduğunu bilmiyordum* (I didn't know she was ill), *Evde olmadığını söyledi* (She said she wasn't at home). *Var* and *yok* become *olduğu* and *olmadığı*: *Arabası olduğunu sanmıyorum* (I don't think he has a car).

head: Kind
Clause
Meaning
rows: that he comes, that he came
that he isn't, wasn't at home
that he has, had a car

blocks.text: **The doer.** A pronoun doer shows only in the possessive ending; you add *benim, senin, onun* for contrast. A noun doer takes the genitive, as with `-mA` in [B1 unit 4](gp-ma-possessive): *Ali'nin geleceğini biliyorum* (I know Ali will come), *Otobüsün geç kaldığını gördüm* (I saw that the bus was late).
**The case** comes from the main verb, exactly as with an ordinary noun object.

blocks.caption: The main verb decides the case
head: Case
Main verbs
Example
rows: *bilmek, söylemek, duymak, görmek, anlamak, öğrenmek, sanmak, unutmak, hatırlamak, fark etmek*
*emin olmak, şüphelenmek, korkmak, bahsetmek, haberi olmak*
*Geç kaldığının farkında değil.* (He isn't aware he's late.)

items.en: I know you'll come.
I heard that Selin has moved.
I didn't know you were ill.
I was very sorry that you didn't come.
I'm sure she's telling the truth.
He promised he wouldn't tell anyone.
I didn't know you had come.

blocks.title: Your coming or his coming?
blocks.text: *Geldiğini* has two readings: *gel-diğ-in-i* (that **you** came) and *gel-diğ-i-n-i* (that **he** came), with the n of [A1 unit 10](gp-pronominal-n). Context usually decides; for clarity add the pronoun: *senin geldiğini*, *onun geldiğini*.

Where English and French put **that** or **que** before the clause, Turkish puts the clause first and the verb last: *Ali'nin geleceğini biliyorum* is, word for word, **Ali's coming-to-be I know**. Turkish also has a borrowed **that**, *ki* (*Biliyorum ki gelecek*), used for emphasis; it comes in [B2 unit 8](gp-ki-conjunction).

You now have two ways to turn a sentence into a noun: `-mA` with a possessive ([B1 unit 4](gp-ma-possessive)) and `-DIk` with a possessive. They aren't interchangeable. `-DIk` presents a **fact**, something true or believed to be true. `-mA` presents an **action**, something wanted, asked for, expected or allowed.

head: What
`-mA`: an action
`-DIk`: a fact
rows: *istemek, beklemek, rica etmek, izin vermek, tavsiye etmek, önermek*
*bilmek, duymak, görmek, anlamak, öğrenmek, sanmak, inanmak, unutmak*

blocks.text: **One verb, two meanings.** A few verbs take both, and the suffix changes the meaning. With *söylemek* and *yazmak*, `-mA` passes on an order and `-DIk` passes on a statement. With *unutmak* and *hatırlamak*, the infinitive is something to do and `-DIk` something that happened.

head: Verb
Action
Fact
rows: *Erken gelmemizi yazdı.* (He wrote that we should come early.)
*Erken geldiğimizi yazdı.* (He wrote that we had come early.)
*Kapıyı kilitlemeyi unuttum.* (I forgot to lock the door.)
*Kapıyı kilitlediğimi unuttum.* (I forgot that I'd locked the door.)

blocks.text: **Feelings take both.** After *sevinmek, üzülmek* and *şaşırmak*, `-DIk` treats the event as a fact and can show its tense, *Geleceğine sevindim* (I'm glad you'll come), while `-mA` simply names the event: *Gelmene sevindim* (I'm glad you came, I'm glad you're coming). Both are correct and common.

items.en: My mother wants me to go to bed early.
My mother thinks I go to bed early.
He told me to wait.
He told me he was waiting.
I'm very glad you came.

blocks.text: Ask yourself what English would say. **Told me to come**, **want you to come**, **asked us to wait**: an action, so `-mA`. **Said that I came**, **know that you came**, **heard that she left**: a fact, so `-DIk`.

*Ali'ye gitmesini söyledim* is **I told Ali to go**; *Ali'ye gittiğini söyledim* is **I told Ali that he had gone**, or that someone else had. Picking the wrong suffix turns an order into a piece of news.

sections.title: Nerede oturduğunu bilmiyorum: questions inside sentences

blocks.text: A question can become part of a larger sentence: **I don't know where she lives**. Turkish keeps the question word where it was and turns the verb into a `-DIk` or `-(y)AcAk` noun with a possessive and the case of the main verb: *Nerede oturuyor?* → *Nerede oturduğunu bilmiyorum*.

head: Direct question
Inside a sentence
Meaning
rows: I don't know where she lives.
I asked when he would come.
I didn't understand what you want.
She didn't say why she was crying.
I don't know how old he is.

blocks.text: **The doer.** *Kim* becomes *kimin* when it is the doer, like any subject of a noun clause: *Kimin geleceğini bilmiyorum* (I don't know who's coming). The other question words stay as they are: *ne, nerede, nereye, ne zaman, nasıl, neden, hangi, kaç*.

**What to do.** `-(y)AcAk` with the possessive of the person who would act gives **what to do, where to go**: *Ne yapacağımı bilmiyorum* (I don't know what to do), *Hangi otobüse bineceğimizi sorduk* (We asked which bus to take).

**Whether.** A yes-or-no question becomes **coming or not coming**: the verb with `-(y)Ip`, then the same verb as a negative noun. Only the second verb carries tense and person: *Gelecek mi?* → *Gelip gelmeyeceğini bilmiyorum* (I don't know whether he'll come); *Evde mi?* → *Evde olup olmadığını sordum* (I asked whether she was at home).

blocks.title: *gelmek*: whether I'll come, whether you'll come…

rows.en: whether he or she will come

blocks.text: **The spoken shortcut.** In conversation a direct question with *diye* ([B1 unit 12](gp-diye-quotative)) is just as common: *Gelecek mi diye sordum* (I asked if he was coming). You'll also hear a question set before the verb with a pause: *Gelecek mi, bilmiyorum*. The noun clause is the form to use in writing.

items.en: I don't know where she lives.
I asked what time the meeting would start.
We still don't know who won.
I don't know what to do.
She asked whether I would come.
I don't remember whether I locked the door.

blocks.text: The question particle *mI* disappears inside a noun clause, and so does the question mark: *Gelip gelmeyeceğini bilmiyorum.* Keep *mI* only with *diye*: *Gelecek mi diye sordum.*
Where English uses **whether** and French **si**, Turkish pairs the positive and the negative: *gelip gelmeyeceğini*, literally **his coming and not coming**.

sections.title: Gelmesini rica etti: passing on requests

blocks.text: In [B1 unit 12](gp-reported-commands-intro) you passed on a request with `-mA` + possessive + accusative and *söylemek*: *Erken gelmemi söyledi* (She told me to come early). The same noun works with every verb of asking. What changes from verb to verb is the case of the person who is asked.

head: Verb
Person asked
Example
rows: *Bana erken gelmemi söyledi.* (She told me to come early.)
*Benden erken gelmemi istedi.* (She asked me to come early.)
*Sizden sessiz olmanızı rica ediyorum.* (I'd ask you to be quiet.)
*Doktor bana dinlenmemi tavsiye etti.* (The doctor advised me to rest.)
*Kaptan herkese gemiden inmesini emretti.* (The captain ordered everyone to leave the ship.)

blocks.title: *beklemek* + *istedi*: she asked me to wait, you to wait…

rows.en: she asked him or her to wait
she asked you to wait (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **Rica etmek** is the polite verb of asking, the same *rica* as in *rica ederim* (you're welcome): *Sizden bir şey rica edeceğim* (I have a favour to ask you). It is the usual verb of formal requests, *Formu doldurmanızı rica ederim* (Please fill in the form), which [B2 unit 5](gp-formal-requests) takes further.

**Not to.** The negative puts a second *-mA* inside: *Geç kalmamamızı rica etti* (She asked us not to be late). **A third person** as the doer takes the genitive: *Müdür herkesin dokuzda gelmesini istedi* (The manager asked everyone to come at nine).
**Quote or report.** *“Lütfen bekleyin.” dedi* becomes *Beklememizi rica etti*. A wish in the third-person imperative, *“Ali de gelsin.” dedi*, becomes *Ali'nin de gelmesini istedi*.

items.en: She asked me to come early.

items.tr: Komşumuzdan müziğin sesini kısmasını rica ettik.
items.seg: Komşumuzdan müziğin sesini kıs|ma|s|ı|n|ı rica ettik.
items.en: We asked our neighbour to turn the music down.
The teacher asked us to switch off our phones.
The doctor advised me to quit smoking.

items.tr: Sizden bu konuyu kimseye anlatmamanızı rica ediyorum.
items.seg: Sizden bu konuyu kimseye anlat|ma|ma|nız|ı rica ediyorum.
items.en: I'd ask you not to tell anyone about this.

blocks.text: *İstemek* with an ablative person means **ask someone to**; with a genitive doer it means **want someone to**: *Ali'den gelmesini istedim* (I asked Ali to come), *Ali'nin gelmesini istiyorum* (I want Ali to come).
*Rica ederim* lives two lives: **you're welcome** after thanks, and **I request** at the end of a formal letter: *Bilgi vermenizi rica ederim* (I would ask you to let me know).

A noun clause can also be the **subject** of a sentence, usually before an adjective such as *önemli, mümkün, doğru, belli* or *kesin*. You already know the pattern from [A2 unit 6](gp-gerek-lazim) and [B1 unit 4](gp-ma-possessive): *Gitmem lazım*, *Gelmene gerek yok*. As a subject, the clause takes no case ending.

**-mA or -DIk, again.** Adjectives that weigh an event, saying whether it matters, is possible, normal or allowed, take `-mA`: *Gelmen önemli* (It's important that you come), *Bunu bu akşam bitirmemiz mümkün değil* (It isn't possible for us to finish this tonight), *Yorgun olman normal* (It's normal that you're tired). Adjectives that say whether something is true or known take `-DIk`: *Ali'nin geleceği kesin* (It's certain that Ali will come), *Haklı olduğun belli* (It's obvious you're right).

head: Clause
Judgment
Meaning
rows: It's not possible for us to finish this tonight.
It's certain that Ali will come.
It isn't clear who will win.

blocks.text: **Questions as subjects.** An embedded question is always `-DIk`: *Ne dediği önemli değil* (What he says doesn't matter), *Kimin kazanacağı belli değil* (It isn't clear who will win).

**Passive verbs of knowing.** News and reports like a `-DIk` clause as the subject of a passive verb ([B1 unit 10](gp-passive)): *Toplantının iptal edildiği açıklandı* (It was announced that the meeting had been cancelled), *Bu kentin çok eski olduğu biliniyor* (This city is known to be very old). *Anlaşılmak*, **to become clear**, works the same way: *Ali'nin haklı olduğu anlaşıldı* (It turned out that Ali was right).

**Feelings as verbs.** A clause can also be the subject of a causative of feeling ([B1 unit 11](gp-causative-objects)): *Onun böyle konuşması beni çok şaşırttı* (Her talking like that really surprised me).

items.en: It's very important that you come too.

items.tr: Bu raporu yarına kadar bitirmemiz imkânsız.
items.seg: Bu raporu yarına kadar bitir|me|miz imkânsız.
items.en: It's impossible for us to finish this report by tomorrow.
Is it true that you're moving?
You're obviously tired.
It isn't clear when she'll be back.
It turned out that Ali was right.

blocks.text: A subject never takes the accusative: *Gelmen önemli*, not *Gelmeni önemli*. Compare *Gelmeni istiyorum*, where the clause is the object of *istiyorum*.
English and French need a dummy subject, **it is important that…**, **il est important que…**. Turkish needs none: the clause itself is the subject, and the adjective comes last.

summary: `-DIk` + possessive + case turns a fact into a noun: *geldiğini biliyorum*, *geldiğine sevindim*, *geldiğinden eminim*; `-(y)AcAk` gives the future, *geleceğini*.
Nouns, adjectives, *var* and *yok* go through *olmak*: *hasta olduğunu*, *arabası olduğunu*, *evde olmadığını*.
`-mA` names an action that is wanted or asked for, `-DIk` a fact that is known or said: *Gelmemi söyledi* (told me to come), *Geldiğimi söyledi* (said I had come).
Embedded questions keep the question word and lose *mI*: *Nerede oturduğunu bilmiyorum*; **whether** is *gelip gelmeyeceğini*.
Requests: *söylemek* + dative person; *istemek* and *rica etmek* + ablative person: *Benden beklememi istedi*, *Sizden sessiz olmanızı rica ediyorum*.
A clause can be the subject, with no case: *Gelmen önemli*, *Haklı olduğun belli*, *Toplantının iptal edildiği açıklandı*.
